text: This is a well-rounded account of the man and his band. It includes some performance footage as well. To me, the music of Sly and the Family Stone is joyful, energetic, exciting music. It is nice to see that music still lives on in many ways.

We literally see the process of how young artists clipped or took beats or bars and interpolated them into new tracks. The process is underlined and emphasized in a way that feels fresh and incredible.

Sly Lives! is not a perfect film, but it’s far more intriguing than many other biographical documentaries. The frank conversations that Questlove captures are stunning, and Sly receives the credit he deserved in life.
An overstuffed treasure chest of musical exploration in addition to being (as the full title suggests) a thoughtful social inquiry.
There's never anything pedantic about this film. [Questlove] wants to share his passion about this particular musical genre and this musician.
This is absolutely extraordinary.

One leaves this fine documentary wondering not only at Sly’s body of work, but at the ripples his career sent through the musical world, paving the way for Janet Jackson, Prince, Parliament/Funkadelic and many others.
The interview style Questlove employs for Sly Lives! Is somewhere between conversational and empathetic, and helps define the film’s tone – it’s informative and thoughtful in equal measure.

An exploration and celebration of Stone’s prodigious talent, but also an attempt to understand his downfall, and to place it in the wider context of being a black artist in America, with all the obstacles and traps that are placed in the way.
Sly Stone defied expectations and pushed boundaries. He challenged the norms of Black American identity, navigating both self-perception and societal acceptance.
What struck me the most was how Questlove concludes the film, turning burden black artists must carry into what is essentially a death sentence.
It confirms Sly's legacy will live on through the discussions the film engenders, ensuring our participation in its preservation.
A fascinating, pulsating documentary that captures a spirit worth following.
It’s a soaring, sometimes-painful journey, but in the end, the music speaks for itself
It goes harder than a typical biography.
Questlove knows how to talk to us normies who love music but who have no idea how it works, and the value he takes in information lifts “Sly Lives!” far above most rock docs.
The culture moves on fast and the standards to which black artists are held are always way more ruthless and higher. I’m just not entirely convinced it lands this thesis as well as it hopes it does.
It’s a great deep dive into a musician’s signature sound, persona, and influence.
Does a great job marshaling both music, archival footage, and interviews and family members and music luminaries, in telling the long life story of Sly Stone

While the various artists help assemble a humanistic picture of the great yet tragically flawed musician, they also bring to mind their own struggles to fit inside that impossible space: entertaining but socially conscious, Black but not too Black.
